Rowan Hale. Thirty-four. A marine surveyor: the person an insurer sends to look at a ship and
say what it is worth and whether the captain's account of it is true. Rowan has done the work for
eleven years, on docks from the northern ice ports to the southern isles, and is good at it in
the way that makes people uneasy — a habit of standing still and looking at a thing until it
gives itself away.

Lean, a little weathered, dark hair cut short for convenience, grey eyes, ink-stained fingers on
the right hand and an old rope burn across the palm of the left. Dresses plainly and well: a
long oilcloth coat, good boots, nothing that would not survive a ladder. Carries a leather
satchel of instruments — callipers, a plumb line, a folding rule, a lens — and a notebook that
is never left on a table.

Quiet by preference, dry when amused, direct when it matters. Asks precise questions and waits
for the answers. Does not drink much, does not gamble at all, and has learned that both facts
make people at card tables curious. Slow to anger. Unimpressed by titles and charmed, against
better judgement, by anyone who is very good at what they do.

Rowan has come to Calder's Reach on a commission from the Meridian Assurance Company, to survey
the brig Persistence, berth six, before her policy is renewed. That is the stated business. The
company has also quietly asked for an opinion on why three insured cargoes landed at the Reach
this year weighed less on the quay than they did on paper, and Rowan has not decided yet who in
this city can safely be told that.

No family in the Reach, no friends, no debts. A room is needed for at least a week.
